description: Held-out group-chat contexts for behavioral-distribution snapshots in the Strathearn Study Group scenario. Each context is a partial chat thread; the agent is asked to write the next message. Contexts span Problems We're Stuck On, Things We Worked Out, Wait Is This True (counterexamples and gotchas), Different Way to See It, What Even Is..., and Off-Topic — to stress-test character differentiation across methodical-convenor / fast-pattern / careful-explainer / abstraction-seeker / alumna-mentor / playful-disrupter / sceptic / newcomer axes.
system_preamble: You are posting in The Study Group, the after-school maths group chat at Strathearn Academy in the East End of Glasgow. Members range from Year 10 to Year 13 plus one alumna. The chat covers problems people are stuck on, things they've worked out, counterexamples, reframings, and the occasional foundational question that the syllabus skipped over. Write your next message in the chat.

Thread: subsets of {1..n} with no two consecutive

Mhairi: I'm pretty sure the count is F(n+2) where F is Fibonacci. Quick check: n=3 gives subsets {}, {1}, {2}, {3}, {1,3} — that's 5 = F(5). I'll write the bijection up properly tomorrow.

Niamh: wait, why is it F(n+2) and not F(n+1)? I always forget which index.

Niamh: Going back over the proof carefully. The induction step assumes n >= 2 implicitly because the swap on line 4 needs two distinct residues. I think n=1 needs a separate one-line check, which is fine but should be stated.

Thread: triangular numbers in Pascal's triangle

Callum: I noticed that 1, 3, 6, 10, 15... shows up as the third diagonal of Pascal's triangle. coincidence or is there a reason?

Mhairi: not a coincidence — T(n) = C(n+1, 2). Standard identity.

Daniyal: ok so the handshake problem (n people, everyone shakes everyone else's hand, count handshakes) and 'how many edges in K_n' — these are LITERALLY the same problem. People are agreeing with me but I don't think they actually believe it.

Ada: point 1: yes Daniyal we get it, both are C(n,2). point 2: what's the new content here.

Thread: sorry probably a stupid question

Thread: wait is this true — sum of three squares

Finn: this might be obvious but — someone in another chat said every positive integer is the sum of three squares. I checked: 7 = 4 + 1 + 1 + 1 needs four. counterexample? or am I missing something about what 'square' means here?

Mhairi: 7 is the standard counterexample, you're right. The theorem is for numbers NOT of the form 4^a(8b+7).

Thread: 'elegance' as an argument

Ada: point 1: I keep seeing people in this chat accept arguments because they're 'elegant' or 'natural'. point 2: elegance is not a proof. point 3: half the time the elegant version skips a case and nobody notices because it sounded good.

Mhairi: name one elegant argument from this chat that skipped a case.

Thread: what even is a function, really

Finn: this might be obvious but — at school we get told a function is 'a rule that takes inputs to outputs', but Eilidh mentioned in passing it's 'a set of ordered pairs', and now I am confused which one is the actual definition.

Daniyal: oh this is a good one. fundamentally the rule version is what you DO with a function, the ordered-pairs version is what a function IS. they're answering different questions.

Thread: trying to guess f(n) from small cases

Callum: f(1)..f(6) by hand: 1, 2, 5, 14, 42, 132. these are the Catalan numbers. so f(7) = 429.

Niamh: nice — before you check, what made you suspect Catalan rather than, say, central binomial coefficients? The first few overlap, and I want to be sure we haven't just matched a prefix.

[Your turn to post]

Thread: hint requested on an Olympiad problem

Mhairi: stuck on Q4 from BMO1 2019. Tried bounding by AM-GM, tried induction, neither lands. Anyone got a hint? I don't want a full solution, just a nudge.

Eilidh: I think this might be one where you want to find an invariant before you try to bound. maybe ask: what quantity stays constant when you do the move the problem describes?

[Your turn to post]

Thread: serious question hidden in a joke proof

Joseph: ok so I have a beautiful proof that 1=2. let a=b. then a^2=ab. then a^2-b^2=ab-b^2. factor: (a-b)(a+b)=b(a-b). divide by (a-b): a+b=b. set a=b=1: 2=1. QED 🎉

Joseph: BUT — hear me out — there's actually a real question hiding in here about when 'divide both sides by x' is and isn't allowed, and I don't think the school answer ('don't divide by zero') is the whole story.
